column4: This answers the question in 82:6 about what could delude a person concerning the generous Lord: He created, formed, and proportioned them, making the question's appeal to divine care concrete.
Continuing the answer to 82:6, this ayah says God assembled the human being in whatever form He willed; the generosity questioned in the section is grounded in deliberate creation.
The section imagines an account that will be opened; this ayah says guardians are assigned over people, introducing the record-keeping that the next verses specify.
This completes 82:10's record-keeping scene: noble writers are appointed, a concrete ledger behind the section's account image.
This completes the writing scene at 82:10–11 by saying the writers know what people do, identifying what enters the record the section says comes due.
After the recording in 82:10–12, this ayah gives the good-doers' outcome as bliss, one side of the recompense account developed by the section.
This completes 82:13's paired outcome by placing the wicked in the Fire, making the record's contrary recompense explicit.
The section's ledger has unpaid rights and withheld aid; this ayah opens with a woe against those who give short measure, a direct scene of withholding what is due.
This specifies one side of the fraud in 83:1: they take full measure from other people, making their own due-counting exact while others' is not.
This completes the measure fraud at 83:2: when they measure or weigh for others, they give less, a concrete reversal of fair settlement.
This follows the fraud in 83:1–3 by asking whether the defrauders think they will be raised, connecting short measure to the final account in the section.
This completes 83:4 by naming the day of resurrection as a great day, giving the accounting warning its horizon.
This introduces the denial described in 83:11: on that day woe is for the deniers, joining corrupt measure to the fate of those who deny the account.
This continues 83:11's portrait of deniers of the Day of Dīn, specifying that only a transgressing sinner denies it; the section likewise joins denial of the account to social failure.
The section names the Day of Dīn as the endpoint of judgment; here Iblīs's curse is said to remain until “يَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” showing that the same day bounds a consequence.

The section pictures the orphan pushed away and the poor person's need unacknowledged; this command says that when one must turn away from people seeking the Lord's mercy, one should address them gently.

The section describes withholding the small benefit that is due; this ayah warns against keeping one's hand tied to the neck and against extending it completely, framing the use of wealth between stinginess and excess.

The section's dictionary form connects dīn with obedience and its first image with an account that comes due; this ayah describes people who fulfill vows and fear a day's evil, joining obligation to the coming reckoning.
Against the section's orphan and poor being denied care, this ayah says the righteous feed food to a needy person, an orphan, and a captive despite their own love of it.
The section's whole surah condemns acts done for display; these feeders say they seek God's face and neither reward nor thanks from people, clarifying the motive opposite to showing off.
The section's surah joins heedless prayer to withholding al-māʿūn; this ayah describes hypocrites who come to prayer lazily and spend only reluctantly, putting both failures together.
This ayah's hypocrites close their hands, forget God, and command wrong while forbidding good; the closed hand is a specific parallel to the section's withholding of aid.
This gives the counter-portrait to 9:67 and the section's refusals: believing men and women establish prayer, give zakāh, and obey God and the Messenger.
This covenant passage joins kindness to orphans and the needy with prayer and zakāh, then says the people turned away; it bundles the very duties the section's actor refuses.

The section's surah condemns prayer and deeds performed to be seen; this ayah says public charity is good, but concealing it while giving to the poor is better, distinguishing visible performance from actual aid.
This opens the portrait completed by 23:2 and 23:4, calling successful the believers whose prayer is humble and who give zakāh—the opposite of the section's distracted prayer and withheld aid.
Against the section's people who are heedless of their prayer, this ayah describes believers as humble in their prayers.
This continues the believer portrait at 23:1–2 and names giving zakāh, the material response missing from the section's portrait.

The section's dictionary form uses d-y-n for human debt as well as recompense; this inheritance rule says shares are determined after any bequest or debt is honored, placing an owed payment before distribution.
This repeats the debt-before-distribution rule in the case of spouses and siblings; it makes the section's literal debt-and-settlement sense concrete in another inheritance context.
